item.stem: In a large city, a recent census found that the proportion of all adult residents who support building a new park is p = 0.40. A student selects a simple random sample of 200 adult residents and finds that 86 support the park, so p̂ = 0.43. The student claims, "The sample proportion is a biased estimator of p, because 0.43 ≠ 0.40." Which response best evaluates the student's claim?

choices.choice_text: The claim is incorrect. For random samples, p̂ is an unbiased estimator of p because the mean of its sampling distribution equals p; individual samples vary around 0.40, so one value of 0.43 reflects sampling variability, not bias.
choices.rationale: Bias describes the estimator's behavior across all possible random samples, not one result. Because the mean of the sampling distribution of p̂ equals p, the estimator does not systematically over- or underestimate p. A single p̂ that differs from 0.40 is expected random variation.

choices.choice_text: The claim is correct. Because 0.43 is greater than 0.40, the sample proportion overestimates p, which shows the estimator is biased upward.
choices.rationale: This judges bias from a single sample result. One p̂ above p is ordinary sampling variability; bias would require p̂ to land above p on average over many random samples, which does not happen for random samples. Fix: Ask whether the mean of p̂ over all possible random samples equals p before calling an estimator biased.

choices.choice_text: The claim is incorrect. Because np = 80 and n(1 − p) = 120 are both at least 10, the sampling distribution of p̂ is approximately normal, so p̂ is unbiased.
choices.rationale: This confuses the large-counts condition with unbiasedness. The large-counts condition concerns the shape of the sampling distribution, while bias concerns its center; p̂ would be unbiased even if the counts were small. Fix: Check the center of the sampling distribution when judging bias, and use large counts only to judge shape.

choices.choice_text: The claim is correct. The bias in p̂ could be eliminated by taking a larger random sample, which would make p̂ equal to 0.40.
choices.rationale: This mixes up bias with variability. A larger sample reduces the spread of the sampling distribution of p̂ but does not change its center, which already equals p; even large samples will rarely give exactly 0.40. Fix: Ask whether a change in sample size affects the center or only the spread before attributing it to bias.

accurate.issue: D's rationale overstates that 'even large samples will rarely give exactly 0.40.' This is not guaranteed for sampling from a finite population: samples approaching the population size can have a substantial probability of matching p exactly, and a census matches p with certainty. Replace this claim with 'A larger sample does not guarantee that p̂ equals p.'

This is not guaranteed for sampling from a finite population; sampling the entire population gives exactly 0.40 with certainty. Replace this with the qualified statement that increasing sample size does not generally guarantee p̂ = p.

item.stem: At a large high school, 40% of all students bike to school, so p = 0.40. A statistics class takes a simple random sample of 50 students and finds that 23 of them bike to school, so p̂ = 0.46. One student says, "The sample proportion is a biased estimator here, because 0.46 ≠ 0.40." Which statement correctly evaluates this claim?

choices.choice_text: The claim is wrong. The difference is sampling variability. p̂ is an unbiased estimator of p because, over all possible random samples of 50, the mean of the p̂ values equals 0.40.
choices.rationale: Unbiasedness describes the sampling distribution, not one sample. The mean of the sampling distribution of p̂ equals p, so p̂ shows no systematic over- or underestimation. Any single random sample can still land above or below p, as 0.46 does here.

choices.choice_text: The claim is correct. Because 0.46 is greater than 0.40, this p̂ overestimated p, which shows that p̂ is a biased estimator of p.
choices.rationale: This judges bias from one sample result. Bias means systematic error across repeated samples. One p̂ that misses p reflects ordinary sampling variability, and the mean of all possible p̂ values is still p. Fix: Ask whether the claim concerns the center of the sampling distribution, not whether one sample's p̂ happened to equal p.

choices.choice_text: The claim cannot be judged from one sample of 50. Bias shrinks as sample size grows, so a larger sample would remove the bias and bring p̂ to 0.40.
choices.rationale: This mixes up bias and variability. A larger n reduces the spread of p̂, since σ_p̂ = √(p(1−p)/n), but it does not change the center. The mean of p̂ equals p at every sample size. Fix: Check which feature of the sampling distribution a change affects: n changes the spread, while bias concerns the center.

choices.choice_text: The claim is wrong, but only because the large-counts condition holds: 50(0.40) = 20 ≥ 10 and 50(0.60) = 30 ≥ 10. With a smaller sample, p̂ would be biased.
choices.rationale: This mixes up the condition for approximate normality with unbiasedness. The large-counts condition decides whether the sampling distribution of p̂ is approximately normal. p̂ is unbiased for p for any random sample size. Fix: Ask what each condition justifies: large counts support a normal shape, and unbiasedness comes from μ_p̂ = p.

accurate.issue: C's rationale presents σ_p̂ = √(p(1−p)/n) as exact for the stated simple random sample from a finite school population. Sampling without replacement requires a finite-population correction for the exact standard deviation. The displayed formula should be qualified as an approximation when the sampling fraction is small; calling the school 'large' does not explicitly establish the 10% condition.

The exact standard deviation includes the finite-population correction √((N−n)/(N−1)). Label the displayed formula an approximation and establish the 10% condition, or omit the formula and explain the decrease in variability qualitatively.

item.stem: A town has 5,000 adult residents, and a recent census found that 60% support a proposed park. A researcher selects a simple random sample of 100 adult residents; all respond accurately, and 54% support the park. Let p be the population proportion who support the park and p̂ be the sample proportion. Which statement correctly identifies the estimator and explains whether the sample result shows bias?

choices.choice_text: The statistic p̂ estimates the parameter p. It is unbiased under this sampling method: across repeated simple random samples, it does not systematically overestimate or underestimate p, even though this sample gives 0.54 rather than 0.60.
choices.rationale: The sample proportion is the statistic used to estimate the town’s population proportion. With simple random sampling and accurate responses from everyone selected, p̂ is unbiased: its average across repeated samples equals p = 0.60. An individual estimate can differ from p because of sampling variability.

choices.choice_text: The statistic p̂ estimates the parameter p, but it is biased downward because 0.54 is less than 0.60.
choices.rationale: Single-sample bias trap: one underestimate does not establish systematic underestimation. Bias describes the estimator’s average behavior across repeated samples, not the direction of one sample’s error. Fix: Ask whether the sampling method systematically underestimates across repeated samples rather than comparing only one estimate with p.

choices.choice_text: The statistic p = 0.60 estimates the parameter p̂ = 0.54, and the difference between them is due to sampling variability.
choices.rationale: Parameter–statistic reversal: p describes all adult residents, so it is the population parameter; p̂ is calculated from the sample, so it is the statistic. The sample statistic estimates the population parameter, not the reverse. Fix: Identify which proportion describes the entire population and which is calculated from the selected sample before naming the estimator.

choices.choice_text: An unbiased p̂ must equal p in every simple random sample, so the result 0.54 shows that this sample could not have been selected randomly.
choices.rationale: Unbiasedness-as-exactness trap: unbiasedness does not require every estimate to equal the parameter. Random samples can produce different proportions; unbiasedness concerns their average, so 0.54 does not contradict simple random sampling. Fix: Separate the requirement that estimates average to p from the incorrect requirement that every estimate equal p.
